extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and scholars of John Milton, historians of political thought and freedom-of-press advocates
extracted.subtask_description: Full text (pamphlet) of John Milton's Areopagitica (1644) arguing against pre-publication licensing and for wide reading and toleration; includes historical examples and policy prescriptions about which books to suppress and how to regulate printing. Useful for analysis of early modern arguments on censorship and freedom of the press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowed grounds for prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: Only two sorts of writings which the Magistrate car'd to take notice of; those either blasphemous and Atheisticall, or Libellous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton cites ancient practice (e.g., Protagoras burnt for atheism; libels punished) to argue that magistrates historically intervened only for blasphemy/atheism or direct defamation (libel). Other sects/opinions and loose writings were generally tolerated. Use these two narrow categories as the legitimate bases for state suppression; avoid broader, catch-all prohibitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Books as living intellectual goods — avoid destruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Books are not absolutely dead things, but doe contain a potencie of life in them to be as active as that soule was whose progeny they are; ... hee who destroyes a good Booke, kills reason it selfe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat books as preservers of intellectual life; destruction or suppression is likened to homicide or martyrdom of ideas. This is a normative principle against censorship: protect books because their loss harms reason and future discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wide reading is essential to virtue and learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Read any books what ever come to thy hands, for thou art sufficient both to judge aright, and to examine each matter. ... the knowledge and survay of vice is in this world so necessary to the constituting of human vertue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton argues readers must be allowed broad access to works (including those with error) because encountering and distinguishing error is necessary to form true judgment and virtuous restraint. Policy implication: permit circulation rather than pre-emptive suppression to foster discernment and discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-publication licencing is dangerous and foreign
rubrics_metrics.description: This project of licencing crept out of the Inquisition, was catcht up by our Prelates, and hath caught some of our Presbyters. ... this order of licencing conduces nothing to the end for which it was fram'd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton traces licensing to the Inquisition and argues it was not an ancient civic practice; he lists practical, moral, and historical objections (suppresses learning, unnatural, likely abused). Use this as a criterion to oppose pre-publication censorship regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer post-publication remedies for libel/mischief
rubrics_metrics.description: Those which otherwise come forth, if they be found mischievous and libellous, the fire and the executioner will be the timeliest and the most effectuall remedy, that mans prevention can use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton endorses dealing with harmful or libellous books after publication (punishment, burning) rather than preventing publication by licence. This supports a policy of accountability post-publication rather than prior restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration of printers/authors (accountability)
rubrics_metrics.description: That no book be Printed, unlesse the Printers and the Authors name, or at least the Printers be register'd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton accepts measures that identify responsible parties (printer/author registration) as a way to hold individuals to account without instituting a censorious licensing bureaucracy. Use registration as a limited regulatory tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing is impractical without total cultural regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: If we think to regulat Printing, thereby to rectifie manners, we must regulat all recreations and pastimes... No musick must be heard, no song be set or sung, but what is grave and Dorick.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument that restricting books would logically require regulating all arts and entertainments to be consistent; therefore licensing is unworkable and disproportionate. Use this point as a pragmatic objection to pre-publication control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppression risks silencing truth and new discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Let her and Falshood grapple; who ever knew Truth put to the wors, in a free and open encounter. Her confuting is the best and surest suppressing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open debate is the criterion for testing ideas: truth will prevail in free encounter. Suppression is likely to prevent discovery and delay correction. Policy should favour free discourse to expose and refute error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of monopolies and corruption in licencing regimes
rubrics_metrics.description: It may be doubted there was in it the fraud of some old patentees and monopolizers in the trade of book-selling; ... brought divers glosing colours to the House.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licensing centralizes power and creates opportunities for monopolists and vested interests to manipulate regulation for profit or suppression. Evaluate proposals by their vulnerability to capture and corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some controversial works require teacher/guide for proper use
rubrics_metrics.description: Those books, & those in great abundance which are likeliest to taint both life and doctrine, cannot be suppresst without the fall of learning, ... such tractats whether false or true are as the Prophesie of Isaiah was to the Eunuch, not to be understood without a guide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton acknowledges that certain works (religious controversies, technical polemics) may be dangerous to the uninstructed and are best approached with guidance. Policy implication: provision of education, commentary, and guidance rather than prohibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary private rejection vs. state coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: As for the burning of those Ephesian books by St. Pauls converts, tis reply'd the books were magick, ... It was a privat act, a voluntary act, and leaves us to a voluntary imitation: the men in remorse burnt those books which were their own; the Magistrat by this example is not appointed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private acts of renunciation or destruction by individuals are distinguished from state-imposed censorship. The criterion is that moral self-discipline and voluntary repudiation are permissible, but state compulsion is not justified by such examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Toleration of non-fundamental differences (within limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: That also which is impious or evil absolutely either against faith or maners no law can possibly permit, ... But those neighboring differences, or rather indifferences, are what I speak of, whether in some point of doctrine or of discipline, which though they may be many, yet need not interrupt the unity of Spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between matters that are absolutely evil (which can be legitimately opposed) and minor doctrinal/disciplinary differences that ought to be tolerated. Use toleration as a guiding principle for dealing with diversity of opinion, except where clear harm or impiety exists.
